english: Let $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and let $S$ be the set of all relations on $A$ that are both symmetric and transitive. Let $p$ be the number of relations in $S$ that are antisymmetric, and let $q$ be the number of relations in $S$ that are not reflexive. Then the value of $p-q$ is ______.
hindi: माना $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ है तथा $S$, $A$ पर उन सभी संबंधों का समुच्चय है जो सममित तथा संक्रामक दोनों हैं। माना $p$, $S$ के उन संबंधों की संख्या है जो प्रतिसममित हैं, तथा $q$, $S$ के उन संबंधों की संख्या है जो स्वतुल्य नहीं हैं। तब $p-q$ का मान ______ है।
solution: For $R\in S$: $(a,b)\in R\Rightarrow(b,a)\in R\Rightarrow(a,a)\in R$ (symmetry, then transitivity)
So with $B$ = set of elements appearing in $R$, $R$ is an equivalence relation on $B$; conversely every equivalence relation on any $B\subseteq A$ is in $S$
Equivalence relations (partitions into classes) on a $k$-element set: $1,1,2,5,15$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$
Symmetric and antisymmetric $\Rightarrow$ no $(a,b)$ with $a\neq b$, so $R\subseteq\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)\}$, and each such $R$ is transitive: $p=2^{4}=16$
solution_full: Let $R\in S$. If $(a,b)\in R$, symmetry gives $(b,a)\in R$, and transitivity applied to $(a,b),(b,a)$ gives $(a,a)\in R$; similarly $(b,b)\in R$.

Let $B$ be the set of elements of $A$ that occur in some pair of $R$. By the previous line $R$ is reflexive on $B$, and it is symmetric and transitive, so $R$ is an equivalence relation on $B$ (and contains no pair with an entry outside $B$).

Conversely, for any $B\subseteq A$ and any equivalence relation on $B$, the same set of pairs is a symmetric and transitive relation on $A$. Different $B$ or different relations give different members of $S$.

An equivalence relation on a set is the same as a partition of the set into equivalence classes. Number of partitions of a $k$-element set: $k=0$: $1$; $k=1$: $1$; $k=2$: $2$; $k=3$: $5$ ($\{abc\}$, three of type $\{ab\}\{c\}$, $\{a\}\{b\}\{c\}$); $k=4$: $15$ ($1$ of type $4$, $4$ of type $3+1$, $3$ of type $2+2$, $6$ of type $2+1+1$, $1$ of type $1+1+1+1$).
$R\in S$ is reflexive iff $B=A$, i.e. $R$ is an equivalence relation on $A$: $15$ relations. Hence $q=52-15=37$.

If $R\in S$ is antisymmetric, a pair $(a,b)$ with $a\neq b$ would force $(b,a)\in R$ by symmetry, contradicting antisymmetry. So $R$ consists of diagonal pairs only. Conversely every subset of $\{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)\}$ is symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive. Hence $p=2^{4}=16$.
originality_note: New: classifying all symmetric-and-transitive relations as equivalence relations on a sub-support (the 'symmetric + transitive implies reflexive' fallacy turned into a count), compared with the antisymmetric ones (way 5: properties of relations linked with counting equivalence classes). Closest known: JEE Main 2024 'symmetric relations that are not reflexive' and 2025-P1-Q8 reflexive symmetric relations with 10 elements. Different because: the count runs over equivalence relations on every subset, and antisymmetry collapses the family to subsets of the diagonal.
blueprint_concepts: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive and antisymmetric relations
Counting reflexive / symmetric / transitive / equivalence relations on a finite set

concept_use.Reflexive, symmetric, transitive and ant: Symmetry plus transitivity forces (a,a) for every element used; symmetry plus antisymmetry leaves only diagonal pairs.
concept_use.Equivalence relations and equivalence cl: Each member of S is an equivalence relation on its support B, counted as partitions of B into classes (1, 1, 2, 5, 15).
concept_use.Counting reflexive / symmetric / transit: n(S) = 52, the 15 reflexive ones and the 16 antisymmetric ones are counted to get p = 16, q = 37.

stem_review: Read as a student: every set, relation and symbol is defined before use, every condition is stated, each sentence has one reading; the answer was recomputed independently in Python by brute-force enumeration, is unique and equals the Answer Plan (negative integer). Changed: No change.
key_step: Seeing that a symmetric transitive relation is an equivalence relation on the set of elements it uses.
justification: Two linked ideas (support decomposition, then partition counts per support) and a numerical answer where one wrong partition count is fatal; easier than 2025-P1-Q8 (L4) because the sets are small. Level 3 before the equivalence-relation adjustment.
